Bel Air chair

Peter Shire’s armchair for Memphis: a fin-shaped back, a bolster arm, and a ball for a foot.

Source
V&A: Bel Air chair (W.19-2010)
Creator
Peter Shire; produced by Memphis
Made
1982; the V&A also records 1984
Style
Memphis (agent-proposed, not yet reviewed by a person)
Moods
Playful, sunny, sculptural, postmodern
Evidence
Downloaded the museum’s published image (843 px wide) from the V&A IIIF server to a private scratchpad and inspected it with the Read tool on 2026-09-25. No image is stored in the catalogue.
Reviewed
25 September 2026
Rights
Link and metadata only. License: unverified. Rights policy

Context

The V&A calls the Bel Air the most important contribution of the Californian designer Peter Shire to Memphis. It was on the cover of Barbara Radice’s widely distributed book on the group and, as a cartoon, on material for the exhibition “Memphis in Memphis” (Memphis Brooks Museum of Art, 1984/85). V&A record.

The record says the asymmetrical back refers to shark fins and to John Lautner’s Stevens House in Malibu, and that the name comes from a Beverly Hills hotel, like other early Memphis titles. The V&A example has the original colors. V&A record.

Materials: painted wood and colored cotton fabric. V&A record.

Observed

  • The back is a tall quarter-circle in deep crimson, rising higher on one side than the other.
  • A lime-green cylinder lies across one arm, and an orange sphere supports the opposite rear corner.
  • The seat cushion is pale mint, the side panel is beige, and the plinth is a pale blue-green block.
  • Each part is a different solid color with no pattern.

Why it belongs

The chair is assembled from primitive solids, a quarter-disc, a cylinder, a sphere, and blocks, each in its own color. This is the toy geometry of Memphis in upholstered form.

Borrow

Build a shape from a few primitive solids and color each one differently.

Break symmetry with one oversized element, such as a quarter-circle or a sphere placed off-axis.
